title: Two fossil hunters' feud named over a hundred dinosaurs and cost them both their fortunes

cover.alt: In the badlands, Edward Drinker Cope in a wide hat and a bearded Othniel Marsh in a bowler shout at each other, each gripping one end of a huge fossil bone.

body: **Edward Drinker Cope** and **Othniel Charles Marsh** began as friends who named fossil species after each other. Then Marsh paid the men at a New Jersey marl pit where they had dug together to send the fossils to him, and in 1870 Cope's mentor Joseph Leidy pointed out that Cope had put the head of his sea reptile *Elasmosaurus* on the end of its tail. For the next two decades the rivals raced each other across the American West, with crews who spied on each other's quarries and who reportedly smashed leftover bones rather than let the other side have them. In 1890 the *New York Herald* printed their quarrel on its front page. Between them they named well over a hundred new dinosaur species, from *Stegosaurus* to *Allosaurus*, though many have not survived later study, and both men spent their fortunes on the race.

slides.alt: A panelled study. Edward Drinker Cope, dark-haired with a moustache and goatee, and Othniel Charles Marsh, balding with a full beard, step towards each other, smiling, to shake hands.
slides.caption: The 1860s. Edward Drinker Cope and Othniel Charles Marsh are friends, who name fossils after each other. Enjoy it.

bubbles.text: I've named a mosasaur after you, Cope!
bubbles.speaker: Othniel Charles Marsh

bubbles.text: How kind! You'll get one too.
bubbles.speaker: Edward Drinker Cope

slides.alt: A long skeleton of a sea reptile stands on a plinth: a very long neck curving up on the right with no head, and the small skull stuck on the short tail at the left. Cope gestures at it proudly; an old grey-haired man points at the neck.
slides.caption: 1868: Cope rebuilds the sea reptile Elasmosaurus and calls it 'flat-tailed'. In 1870 his mentor Joseph Leidy takes a look.

bubbles.text: Edward... that's its neck. The head goes on the other end.
bubbles.speaker: Joseph Leidy

slides.alt: Cope staggers under a teetering stack of journals, sweating and looking over his shoulder.
slides.caption: Cope tries to buy back every copy of the journal with his mistake, and reprints it with the head at the front.

slides.alt: By a green marl pit, Marsh, in a bowler hat, smirks as he hands a wad of banknotes to a grinning quarryman in braces.
slides.caption: Marsh, meanwhile, pays the men at a New Jersey marl pit they've dug together to send the fossils to him.

bubbles.text: Anything you find, you send to me. Not to Cope.
bubbles.speaker: Othniel Charles Marsh

slides.alt: In the striped badlands, a digger in a slouch hat grins as he brings a sledgehammer down on a fossil bone, splinters flying.
slides.caption: The race moves west. At Como Bluff, Wyoming, Marsh's man reports smashing leftover bones so Cope can't have them.

bubbles.text: If we can't have it, nobody can.
bubbles.speaker: A digger

slides.alt: A man in braces peers through a spyglass from behind a rock at a distant digger working on a bone.
slides.caption: Spies everywhere. One of Marsh's diggers defects to Cope and locks his old partner out of the station.

bubbles.text: Nobody suspects a man behind a rock.
bubbles.speaker: A spy

slides.alt: A giant newspaper with a picture of two bearded scientists shouting. A man in a bowler laughs at it; a woman in purple stares.
slides.caption: 12 January 1890. The New York Herald puts the feud on its front page: 'Scientists wage bitter warfare'.

bubbles.text: Two professors fighting over old bones. Wonderful.
bubbles.speaker: A reader

slides.alt: Cope and Marsh glare at each other across the study, each with a heap of fossil bones at his feet.
slides.caption: Final score: Marsh 80 new dinosaurs, Cope 56. Both spend their fortunes. Marsh dies with $186 in the bank.

slides.question: Cope's Elasmosaurus platyurus means 'flat-tailed'. What was its 'tail'?
slides.explanation: He put the skull on the wrong end. The long 'tail' was the neck; Joseph Leidy pointed it out in 1870.
